title: Chicagohenge! When the Sun Lines Up With City Streets
summary: Have you ever seen the sun line up perfectly with a street? In Chicago, it happens twice a year. When the fall equinox arrives on September 22, the sun rises and sets straight down streets that run east and west. Between the tall buildings downtown, the sun looks like it's framed by a giant picture frame. People call it "Chicagohenge" — a nickname inspired by Stonehenge, the ancient stone circle in England that also lines up with the sun. "In Chicago's canyon of tall buildings, the sun will be framed by the rising sun, and the setting sun will be framed by those tall buildings," says Michelle Nichols of the Adler Planetarium. Why does it happen? Chicago's streets follow the compass — north, south, east, and west. That grid pattern came from 19th-century planning, when grids made it easier to buy and sell land. Denver is another good city for spotting it. Long ago, cities like Tenochtitlan, the Aztec ancestor of Mexico City, were built to match the stars on purpose. Today it's more of an accident — but it still feels special. "The sky really is still up there," Nichols says.
why_it_matters: Knowing how streets and the sun can line up helps you notice patterns in the sky over your own neighborhood — and shows that city design and nature can meet by accident.

background_read: Stonehenge (an ancient circle of giant stones in England) is thousands of years old and lines up with the sun at certain times of year, which may be why people gathered there.
An equinox happens twice a year, in spring and fall, when day and night are almost exactly the same length.
New York City has its own version of this event, called Manhattanhenge, when the sun lines up with the city's east-west streets.
Article_Structure: WHO: People in Chicago watching the sky, plus expert Michelle Nichols of the Adler Planetarium.
WHAT: Twice a year, at the fall equinox on September 22, the sun rises and sets straight down Chicago's east-west streets — a sight nicknamed 'Chicagohenge.'
WHERE: Downtown Chicago, framed between tall buildings; Denver is another city where people can spot it.
WHY: Chicago's streets follow a north-south, east-west grid planned in the 19th century, so at the equinox the sun lines up perfectly with them.

perspectives.description: This is a free, beautiful show that anyone in the city can enjoy just by looking down the street at the right time.
The grid was made for buying and selling land long ago, not for the sun, so the alignment is really a lucky accident of city design.
Events like this are a fun reminder, as Michelle Nichols says, that the sky is still up there for everyone to notice and learn about.
